title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
summary: Risk-stratify before cytoreductive therapy by malignancy biology, disease burden, baseline uric acid, renal function, and treatment potency; use hydration, urate lowering, and intensive biochemical surveillance to prevent arrhythmia, acute kidney injury, and dialysis-requiring metabolic collapse.
seoDescription: Physician guide to tumor lysis syndrome risk assessment, Cairo-Bishop criteria, hydration, urate-lowering prophylaxis, monitoring, and escalation.
clinicalQuestion: Which patients require intensive tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis and monitoring before or during cancer treatment?
keyTakeaways: Treat TLS prevention as part of the treatment plan before cytoreduction in patients with highly proliferative, chemosensitive hematologic malignancy, high disease burden, elevated baseline uric acid, or impaired kidney function. [5][18][22]

Laboratory TLS is defined by metabolic derangements including uric acid at least 8.0 mg/dL and potassium at least 6.0 mEq/L; clinical TLS adds acute kidney injury, arrhythmia/sudden death, or seizure. [1][4]

Hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase is the core preventive strategy; reserve rasburicase for patients with high-risk features or clinically consequential hyperuricemia and avoid it in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. [11][16][18]
Do not dismiss TLS before therapy: spontaneous TLS can reveal previously undiagnosed hematologic malignancy and can occur, less commonly, with solid tumors. [1][13][14][21]

sections.heading: Identify patients who need tumor lysis prophylaxis before therapy
sections.intro: Risk is driven by tumor kinetics, burden, host clearance capacity, and anticipated treatment response.
paragraphs: Initiate a TLS prevention plan before cytotoxic, targeted, or cellular therapy when the malignancy is highly proliferative and treatment-sensitive, particularly in hematologic cancer with high disease burden. Hematologic malignancy and high tumor burden confer the highest recognized risk; TLS is also reported after immunotherapy and CAR T-cell therapy, with a systematic review reporting incidences ranging from no recorded events with ofatumumab to as high as 10% with CAR T-cell therapies. [5][11][12][22]

Use baseline tumor burden and biochemical reserve to intensify prophylaxis. Features associated with high risk include high proliferative rate, elevated baseline uric acid, large tumor burden, chemosensitive disease, and leukocyte count greater than 50 × 10^9/L; kidney dysfunction increases the consequence of urate and phosphate accumulation. [18][22]

For acute myeloid leukemia receiving induction therapy, male sex, increased circulating blasts, elevated baseline uric acid, and IDH1/2 mutation were independent TLS risk factors in a retrospective cohort; venetoclax-based therapy showed a trend toward increased risk. These data support lower thresholds for intensive surveillance when several risk features coexist rather than reliance on leukemia diagnosis alone. [20]
bullets: Before treatment in a patient at meaningful risk, obtain serum uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine, and lactate dehydrogenase; use abnormalities to establish a baseline and identify evolving spontaneous TLS. [1][22]

Assess volume status and urine output before prescribing prophylactic fluids; adequate urine output was associated with lower TLS risk in AML, whereas excessive positive fluid balance correlated with severe TLS. [20]

Plan the location of care before treatment: patients with active electrolyte derangement, oliguria/anuria, acute kidney injury, or anticipated rapid cytoreduction require a monitored setting capable of frequent laboratory testing and urgent renal replacement therapy if needed. [1][18][22]

table.caption: Practical pre-treatment factors that increase prophylaxis and monitoring intensity. [5][18][20][22]
rows: Tumor biology
Highly proliferative, treatment-sensitive hematologic malignancy [12][18]
Use prophylactic hydration and urate-lowering therapy before cytoreduction. [11][18]
Tumor burden
Large tumor burden or leukocyte count >50 × 10^9/L [18]
Escalate to intensive biochemical surveillance and consider rasburicase-based urate control when hyperuricemia risk is high. [11][18]
Baseline chemistry
Elevated uric acid, potassium, phosphate, creatinine, or lactate dehydrogenase [1][18]
Treat as active or evolving metabolic risk; do not wait for additional cytoreduction to begin supportive management. [1][22]
Host factors
Kidney dysfunction, oliguria, or inability to tolerate excess volume [1][20][22]
Individualize fluid delivery, monitor output closely, and arrange early nephrology support if metabolic abnormalities progress. [20][22]
Treatment modality
Immunotherapy or CAR T-cell therapy in high-burden hematologic cancer [5]
Continue TLS surveillance after treatment initiation; risk is not limited to conventional chemotherapy. [5]

sections.heading: Recognize laboratory TLS before cardiac, neurologic, or renal complications develop
sections.intro: Interpret serial metabolic values with kidney function and clinical events rather than as isolated abnormalities.
paragraphs: Use modified Cairo-Bishop criteria to classify laboratory TLS: uric acid at least 8.0 mg/dL, potassium at least 6.0 mEq/L, and abnormalities in phosphate and calcium are the defining metabolic pattern. Clinical TLS requires laboratory evidence plus acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmia or sudden death, or seizure; acute kidney injury is defined in the cited modified criteria as creatinine greater than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal for age and sex. [1][4]

A rising uric acid concentration with elevated lactate dehydrogenase and nonobstructive oliguric or anuric acute kidney injury before cytotoxic therapy should prompt evaluation for spontaneous TLS and occult or progressive malignancy. One proposed spontaneous TLS framework uses uric acid at least 8.0 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase more than twice the upper limit of normal, and acute nonpostobstructive oliguric or anuric renal failure. [1]

Do not require hyperphosphatemia to recognize spontaneous TLS. Phosphate may be reutilized by rapidly proliferating tumor cells and therefore can be less conspicuous in spontaneous TLS, whereas hyperphosphatemia is more typical after rapid therapy-induced tumor killing. [1]
bullets: Obtain an ECG immediately for potassium elevation or symptoms suggesting arrhythmia; arrhythmia is a clinical TLS criterion and hyperkalemia from massive tissue breakdown is specifically recognized in kidney disease guidance. [4][23]
Interpret acute kidney injury as both a clinical TLS complication and a risk amplifier because impaired renal clearance worsens urate and electrolyte accumulation. [1][22]

Evaluate alternative contributors to hyperkalemia or acute kidney injury while treating suspected TLS, including dehydration, hyperglycemia, insulin deficiency, beta-adrenergic blockade, aldosterone blockade, and other causes of massive tissue breakdown. [23]

table.caption: TLS classification and immediate implication. [1][4]
rows: Laboratory TLS
Metabolic TLS pattern; cited thresholds include uric acid ≥8.0 mg/dL and potassium ≥6.0 mEq/L. [1]
Begin or intensify hydration, urate-lowering therapy, and serial electrolyte/renal monitoring. [11][18]
Clinical TLS
Laboratory TLS plus creatinine >1.5× upper limit of normal, arrhythmia/sudden death, or seizure. [1][4]
Manage as an oncologic emergency with cardiac monitoring and urgent escalation for kidney replacement therapy when indicated by refractory metabolic complications. [18][22]
Spontaneous TLS
TLS biochemical and clinical pattern before cytotoxic therapy; uric acid ≥8.0 mg/dL, LDH >2× upper limit of normal, and nonobstructive oliguric/anuric AKI support the diagnosis. [1]
Search for underlying hematologic malignancy or high-burden solid tumor while immediately treating the metabolic emergency. [1][13][21]

sections.heading: Choose hydration and urate-lowering prophylaxis by hyperuricemia risk
sections.intro: Pair volume management with a urate-lowering strategy before anticipated rapid tumor kill.
paragraphs: Use intravenous hydration, laboratory monitoring, and allopurinol or rasburicase as the core prophylactic bundle for high-risk patients. Hydration supports urinary clearance, but fluid administration must be titrated to urine output and cardiopulmonary tolerance; excessive positive fluid balance correlated with severe TLS in an AML cohort. [11][20]

Use allopurinol when prevention of additional uric acid formation is appropriate and the patient can take oral therapy; oral doses reported for TLS range up to 800 mg/day. Intravenous allopurinol is an option when oral administration is not feasible. [18]

Favor intravenous rasburicase for patients with high proliferative tumors, high baseline uric acid, large tumor burden, high-risk chemosensitive disease, or when rapid reduction of existing hyperuricemia is required. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase indicated for prophylaxis and treatment of chemotherapy-associated hyperuricemia in hemato-oncology patients at risk for TLS. [16][18]

Do not administer rasburicase in known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia have occurred after exposure, and G6PD deficiency is a contraindication. [16]
bullets: When institutional practice uses fixed-dose rasburicase, retrospective comparative data found similar 24-hour uric acid treatment success with single 3 mg, 6 mg, and 7.5 mg doses and weight-based dosing; 6 mg produced lower sustained uric acid concentrations than 3 mg. [17]

A fixed-dose approach is supported by comparative observational data, not by equivalence to every clinical scenario; reassess uric acid and the full TLS metabolic panel after administration and redose only according to local protocol and the evolving clinical picture. [17]

Avoid treating uric acid in isolation: potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine, urine output, and ECG findings determine whether prophylaxis remains adequate or emergency management is required. [1][4][23]

subsections.heading: Allopurinol versus rasburicase
paragraphs: The practical distinction is timing and urgency: allopurinol prevents formation of new uric acid, whereas rasburicase is used when high-risk features or established hyperuricemia call for rapid urate reduction. Choose rasburicase only after addressing the G6PD contraindication; choose intravenous allopurinol when allopurinol is indicated but oral delivery is not possible. [16][18]

table.caption: Urate-lowering selection for TLS prevention or treatment. [16][17][18]
rows: Allopurinol
Prevention of hyperuricemia in TLS; may be used intravenously when oral therapy cannot be given. [18]
Oral TLS dosing reported up to 800 mg/day. [18]
Does not provide the rapid urate removal sought in high-risk or established hyperuricemia scenarios. [16][18]
Rasburicase
Prophylaxis or treatment of hyperuricemia during chemotherapy in hemato-oncology patients at TLS risk; particularly useful with high-risk clinical features. [16][18]
Comparative fixed single doses of 3 mg, 6 mg, and 7.5 mg had similar 24-hour uric acid treatment success to weight-based dosing; 6 mg had lower sustained uric acid than 3 mg. [17]
Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because of hemolysis and methemoglobinemia risk. [16]

sections.heading: Monitor frequently and escalate when complications emerge
sections.intro: The transition from biochemical TLS to clinical TLS is defined by organ-threatening complications.
paragraphs: For high-risk AML after treatment initiation, a retrospective study recommended electrolyte monitoring every 6 hours for 72 hours. Apply similarly intensive serial monitoring when rapid tumor kill is anticipated, baseline chemistry is abnormal, or treatment includes modalities associated with abrupt response; follow uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine, and urine output together. [20][5]

Escalate immediately for potassium at least 6.0 mEq/L, ECG change, arrhythmia, seizure, progressive oliguria/anuria, or acute kidney injury meeting clinical TLS criteria. These findings indicate clinical TLS or imminent clinical TLS and require monitored management rather than outpatient observation. [1][4][23]

Engage nephrology early when acute kidney injury progresses despite fluid and metabolic management or when electrolyte abnormalities are refractory. TLS is a hemato-oncologic emergency associated with spontaneous or therapy-induced cell death and can require kidney replacement therapy for severe metabolic and renal complications. [18][22]
bullets: Use continuous or repeated ECG assessment for clinically significant hyperkalemia because arrhythmia and sudden death define clinical TLS. [4][23]
Track fluid balance as a treatment endpoint, not merely fluid intake; preserve urine output while avoiding excessive positive balance. [20]

Coordinate cytoreductive therapy with the oncology team once emergency metabolic control and monitoring capability are established; ongoing tumor lysis can continue after initiation of highly effective therapy. [5][22]

table.caption: Escalation triggers during TLS surveillance. [1][4][20][23]
rows: Potassium ≥6.0 mEq/L [1]
Meets a cited laboratory TLS threshold and carries arrhythmic risk. [1][4]
Obtain ECG, initiate urgent hyperkalemia management, and use monitored care. [4][23]
Creatinine >1.5× upper limit of normal [1][4]
Meets the cited acute kidney injury criterion for clinical TLS when laboratory TLS is present. [1][4]
Intensify monitoring, reassess volume status and urine output, and obtain early nephrology input if worsening. [20][22]
Arrhythmia, sudden death, or seizure [4]
Clinical TLS complication. [4]
Provide emergency monitored management and urgent specialty escalation. [4][18]
Oliguria or anuria with hyperuricemia and elevated LDH before treatment [1]
Suggests spontaneous TLS after exclusion of obstructive renal failure. [1]
Treat the metabolic emergency and investigate occult or progressive malignancy. [1][14]

sections.heading: Recognize spontaneous TLS and TLS beyond conventional chemotherapy
sections.intro: Absence of recent cytotoxic chemotherapy does not exclude TLS.
paragraphs: Suspect spontaneous TLS in a patient with unexplained hyperuricemia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, acute nonobstructive oliguria/anuria, and a compatible electrolyte pattern before therapy. Spontaneous TLS may be the first presentation of previously unrecognized chronic lymphocytic leukemia and has also been reported in solid tumors. [1][3][13][14][21]

In spontaneous TLS, phosphate may be normal despite substantial lysis because proliferating tumor cells can reutilize released phosphate. Therefore, a normal phosphate concentration should not delay treatment when hyperuricemia, kidney injury, potassium abnormality, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase support the diagnosis. [1]

Continue TLS risk assessment with newer immune-based therapies. TLS is a recognized toxicity of immunotherapies, especially in hematologic malignancy with high disease burden, and CAR T-cell therapy has reported TLS rates up to 10% in a systematic review. [5]
bullets: Exclude postrenal obstruction when oliguria or anuria is present before attributing renal failure to spontaneous TLS. [1]
When TLS precedes a cancer diagnosis, urgently pursue the underlying malignancy while treating hyperuricemia, electrolyte abnormalities, and kidney injury in parallel. [1][14]
In solid tumors, maintain suspicion when disease burden is high and metabolic findings fit TLS; the condition is less common than in hematologic malignancy but potentially fatal. [13][21]

table.caption: Patterns that should prevent false reassurance in suspected TLS. [1][5][13][21]
rows: No recent chemotherapy
TLS may occur spontaneously before diagnosis or treatment. [1][14]
Evaluate for spontaneous TLS and underlying malignancy. [1]
Normal or modest phosphate in suspected spontaneous TLS
Released phosphate may be reutilized by proliferating tumor cells. [1]
Base action on the integrated uric acid, potassium, kidney function, LDH, and clinical pattern. [1]
Solid tumor diagnosis
TLS is less common but reported and potentially fatal in solid tumors. [13][21]
Use the same metabolic emergency framework when the biochemical pattern is present. [13]
Non-chemotherapy immune treatment
TLS is a recognized immunotherapy toxicity, especially with high-burden hematologic malignancy. [5]
Maintain post-treatment biochemical surveillance and prophylaxis appropriate to tumor burden and baseline risk. [5][11]
